summary:
Macau is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China. It stands under the national framework of the Basic Law and administers its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation.

Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, and the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offences identically. The general age of consent is 14 for both. Penal Code Article 166 prescribes 3 to 10 years' imprisonment for anal intercourse with a person under 14, and up to 4 years where a 14-to-16-year-old's inexperience is taken advantage of.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Services Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on Macau identity cards, and the gender-marker-change study carried out in 2015 never produced legislation. Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the bureau received eight written requests to change gender on identity documents; all were rejected.

In April 2026 the Legal Affairs Bureau (Direcção dos Serviços de Assuntos de Justiça) said there are "no plans" to revise the framework, pending "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family relations. The UN Human Rights Committee noted in 2017 that Macau still does not allow transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents.

The absence of a marker-change route produces border-crossing confusion. A trans man holding a Hong Kong identity card marked male remains registered female in Macau, so his documents disagree at the frontier.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. A March 2013 bill by Legislative Assembly member José Pereira Coutinho to give same-sex civil unions the same rights as heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions and expressly excluded the right to adopt. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples.

Domestic-violence legislation excludes relationships the law classes as same-sex, because same-sex partners are not treated as "family members". A 2011 public consultation had included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope; the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and in 2016 it insisted on the exclusion. Rainbow of Macau complained to the UN Committee against Torture in October 2015, which urged Macau to protect all domestic-violence victims "without discrimination"; the group said the enacted law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

Sexual orientation is absent from the non-exhaustive list of prohibited discrimination grounds in Basic Law Article 25. Sectoral protections exist in employment (Law No. 7/2008, Article 6/2, fines up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker), personal data (Law No. 8/2005) and the ombudsman (Law No. 4/2012); each is framed around sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Macau is the only area in China without identity gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions; both are available in mainland China and Hong Kong.

On 9 June 2015 the newspaper Exmoo ran a front-page story about a high school student alleged to have molested a 9-year-old, calling the perpetrator a "gay demon" (基魔). Rainbow of Macau spokesperson Jason Chao responded that the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offenders identically.

The Macau LGBT Rights Concern Group was created in late 2012 and Rainbow of Macau registered in April 2013; gay culture in Macau remains mostly invisible.
localsOnly:
In February 2015 Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on Macau identity documents; one individual, speaking behind a screen under the name Avery, sought the change. It was the first organised push for gender recognition in Macau.

In February 2015 a transgender student, Avery (pseudonym), told Macau media about abuse and bullying experienced while studying at a local school.

On 16 August 2018 the deputy director of the Education and Youth Affairs Bureau (DSEJ), Leong Vai Kei, said students with "indications of homosexuality" would be referred to doctors or psychologists for medical examination. She later apologised, claiming misquotation and mistranslation from Cantonese.

On 31 March 2026 four trans residents appealed to the Justice Services Direction for legal recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source addresses whether gender expression is criminalised; the Penal Code's identical treatment of homosexual and heterosexual offences is the only sourced statement on the criminal law's scope.

The content and findings of the 2015 gender-marker-change study are not in the sourced material; only that it produced no legislation.

Whether the eight rejected identity-document requests included applications from non-residents is not stated.

Enforcement data on the domestic-violence law's application to same-sex or transgender victims is not sourced.

No sourced figures on prosecution or sentencing for violence against transgender people in Macau.

Whether the sectoral anti-discrimination laws (employment, personal data, ombudsman) extend to gender identity is not stated; the sourced descriptions frame them around sexual orientation.
